items.title: Three Decades into Dernière Volonté, Geoffroy D. Revisits His Early Sound on “Cendre” — Hear Him in Conversation with Phil Blackmarquis
items.summary: Ashes are what remain when the fire has finished its work, when the heat has departed and the substance of a former life has been reduced to a fine grey… The post Three Decades into Dernière Volonté, Geoffroy D. Revisits His Early Sound on “Cendre” — Hear Him
items.fullText:
Ashes are what remain when the fire has finished its work, when the heat has departed and the substance of a former life has been reduced to a fine grey residue. The outline of a face in an old photograph, the scent of a room abandoned decades earlier, or the sudden recognition of a voice once intimately familiar can summon an entire world from the smallest surviving fragment. Memory has a strange relationship with decay, preserving certain impressions with exquisite precision while allowing entire years to vanish into obscurity. Perhaps ruins have such a hold on the imagination because their empty rooms invite us to picture everything that once filled them.

For nearly three decades, French musician Geoffroy D. has explored similarly desolate territory through Dernière Volonté, whose music often suggests the solemn grandeur of abandoned cathedrals and military processions. His new album, Cendre, takes its title from the French word for ash. On WAVES #549, Brussels DJ and broadcaster Phil Blackmarquis talks with Geoffroy about the old instruments he brought back into the studio and the friends he remembers in these songs.

Geoffroy began the project in the mid-1990s, working in martial industrial and dark ambient with ceremonial percussion, austere electronics, and distant melodic phrases. A decisive turn came with 2003’s Les Blessures de l’ombre and 2006’s Devant le miroir, when organs and neoclassical arrangements brought out the tenderness in his melodies. The records sit somewhere between the stately romanticism of Dead Can Dance and the French electronic sensibilities of Taxi Girl, with Geoffroy’s restrained vocals at the center of songs about love, loss, and the passage of time.

From 2019 onward, drum machines and arpeggiators drew Dernière Volonté closer to his electronic project Position Parallèle. On Cendre, he returns to the neoclassical darkwave of those earlier records, with funeral organs and solemn rhythms back in the foreground. “Maudits” has the snap of a club track, and “Ombres” changes direction late in the song before settling into a figure that repeats to the end. Even at their fullest, the arrangements leave room for the close, measured sound of Geoffroy’s voice.

Silences et Grésillements released the twelve-track Cendre on September 25, 2026. Tesco Distribution carries the CD, black vinyl, and a translucent crystal-blue pressing limited to 250 copies.

Order Cendre here or listen on Apple Music or Spotify.

Dernière Volonté on WAVES #549

In the October 20 episode, first aired on Brussels’ Radio Panik, Geoffroy describes Cendre as the last part of a trilogy about decline and says Dernière Volonté will carry on. An early title borrowed the opening of a Pierre Motin poem, “Souviens-toi que tu n’es que cendre,” or “Remember that you are but ashes.” Geoffroy tells Blackmarquis that he had tired of the arpeggiators and drum machines he’d used on the previous records. Returning to older synthesizers and samplers let him work orchestral and folk sounds back into the songs and give Dernière Volonté and Position Parallèle distinct identities again.

“L’âne et le roi” gave the album its direction when Geoffroy paired an operatic excerpt with Jacques Prévert’s “Chanson du mois de mai.” “Harmonies du soir” takes him back to Paris in the 1990s, while the choir-like voices in “Vanités” came from samples he manipulated in the studio. The rivers in “Ombres” come from walks around Angoulême, where thoughts about humanity’s decline take a personal turn as he considers where he’d like to spend the end of his life.

Geoffroy dedicates “Célébration” to Stéphane of Nuit et Brouillard. The conversation also turns to the death of Albin Julius and how losing friends has altered Geoffroy’s work. Getting the new songs to sit together took months of revisions. He’d already reached the mastering stage when he went back to recording and mixing, and he explains why he prefers to keep that work in his own hands.

Blackmarquis also previews Orages & Miséricordes, a companion release that continues the dark ambient work of Dernière Volonté’s 1998 debut, Obéir et Mourir. Geoffroy drew on material from old tapes and newer recordings for the instrumental double album. Geoffroy self-released it in a double-CD edition of 199 copies. Order Orages & Miséricordes from Tesco.

After asking Geoffroy about his September set at Tower Transmissions in Dresden and his impatience with long tours, Blackmarquis switches to a blind listening test. It starts about 38 minutes into the English edition. Taxi Girl and Depeche Mode take Geoffroy back to records he heard as a child, and a selection from Oxygène gets him talking about why he keeps returning to Jean-Michel Jarre’s Équinoxe. Shriekback’s “The Big Hush” brings up Michael Mann’s Manhunter, while a Nico track gets the two of them talking about Dead Can Dance.

Blackmarquis founded Brussels’ DARKOTHEQUE parties, where he DJs, and co-hosts WAVES with Fernando Wax. The show has been on the air since 2014, covering post-punk, minimal synth, new wave and EBM, with guests including Peter Hook, Gary Numan and The Hacker. Blackmarquis and Wax also lead the team behind Red Maze Records and curate its My Precious! compilations. Their fifth volume brings together exclusives and unreleased tracks from artists including Antiflvx and Extra Bleu Ciel. Listen to My Precious! Vol. 5.

items.title: Conjecture’s ‘Through Swords And Spears, I Seek Infinity’ arrives 18 December
items.summary: Conjecture's new album 'Through Swords And Spears, I Seek Infinity' is out 18 December on Cyclic Law, pairing industrial and neoclassical arrangements.
items.fullText:
Greek industrial project “Through Swords And Spears, I Seek Infinity,” the new album by Conjecture, is released on 18 December through Cyclic Law. A free Bandcamp listening party for the album takes place on 16 December at 7 PM CET.

The label describes the album as an exploration of heroism through the idea of “Divine Annihilation,” the conscious surrender and dissolution of the self in pursuit of an absolute reality beyond the limits of human existence. Musically, it takes a more austere and intense direction within Conjecture’s industrial vocabulary, pairing forceful industrial structures with neoclassical arrangements, atmospheric layers and ritualistic elements, with vocals shifting between declaration, invocation and raw outburst.

The album runs eight tracks at 44:50 and is released as a CD edition of 200 copies in a 6-panel digisleeve with matte lamination. Two tracks, “Deposition” and “Eclipse,” are streaming now as part of the Bandcamp pre-order.

About Conjecture

Vasilis Angelopoulos is the Greek musician behind Conjecture, a solo project that marked ten years of activity in 2024. The project blends minimal-electro, dark-ambient, industrial and cinematic influences and has released productions through labels including Ars Nocturna, Raumklang Music and Zoharum. In 2023, “Nostalgia Futura” became Conjecture’s first release for Cyclic Law, exploring the psychological phenomenon of anticipatory nostalgia. The following year, Zoharum reissued “V” for the project’s tenth anniversary, adding tracks from the 2020 EP “∫V” plus remixes by Antechamber, Evitceles, Flint Glass and Blakk Harbor.

“Through Swords And Spears, I Seek Infinity” is Conjecture’s second album for Cyclic Law.

items.title: Beckahesten’s ‘Rovet’ is the trio’s final album with Viktoria Rolandsdotter
items.summary: Beckahesten's new album 'Rovet' is out 18 December on Cyclic Law as CD and vinyl, marking the Swedish trio's final collaboration with Viktoria Rolandsdotter.
items.fullText:
Swedish trio Beckahesten releases its fourth album, “Rovet,” on 18 December through Cyclic Law, marking the group’s final collaboration with vocalist Viktoria Rolandsdotter. A free Bandcamp listening party for the album takes place on 15 December at 7 PM CET.

“Rovet” is described by the label as seven tales told around a blazing fire, with something “ghastly always lurking in the surrounding darkness.” The album moves across meadows and forests to the sound of distant calls and tribal drums, with ring-dance rhythms set against sparse strings and sombre drones, before a ship arrives at the shore carrying “unwelcome cargo” that leads the village down into the valley of the dead.

The album runs seven tracks at 37:47 and is released on CD (200 copies, 6-panel digisleeve) and black vinyl (250 copies, printed inner sleeve, matte varnish). Two tracks, “Kallad” and “Heden,” are streaming now as part of the Bandcamp pre-order.

About Beckahesten

Beckahesten is a Swedish trio set up by Peo Bengtsson, Per Åhlund and vocalist Viktoria Rolandsdotter. Åhlund has also been active with Sophia, Skare and Diskrepant, and as a live member of Karjalan Sissit. The band’s name is drawn from Nordic folklore: a water spirit that tricks people into riding on its back before pulling them under, growing longer the more riders it carries, with an equivalent in the Scottish water kelpie.

The trio released its debut album, “Vattenhålens Dräpare,” in 2020, followed by “Tydor” in 2021 and the single “Midvinter” the same year. Side-Line interviewed the band around that period. Third album “Svältens Tid” followed in 2024, also released on vinyl. “Rovet” is Beckahesten’s fourth album and the last to feature Rolandsdotter as vocalist.

items.title: Corona Barathri’s ‘Immersio in Caliginem’ arrives 18 December on Cyclic Law
items.summary: Corona Barathri's new album 'Immersio in Caliginem' is out 18 December on Cyclic Law, preceded by a free Bandcamp listening party on 13 December.
items.fullText:
Russian ritual and dark-ambient project “Immersio in Caliginem”, the new album by Corona Barathri, is released on 18 December on Cyclic Law. A free Bandcamp listening party for the album takes place five days earlier, on 13 December at 7 PM CET.

The album is structured as seven tracks across 64 minutes, described by Cyclic Law as a descent through seven rituals guided by the figure of Belial toward the “abode of Mother Nahemah.” It is the first Corona Barathri release to feature new project members Tania Geisler and Alexandra Fauho, alongside guest contributions from Chthonia, Erszebeth, Ashtoreth and New Risen Throne. The CD edition is limited to 200 copies in a 6-panel digisleeve.

Two tracks from the album, “Cor Unum, Essentia Una Sumus” and “Enixus in Tenebris,” are streaming now as part of the Bandcamp pre-order.

About Corona Barathri

Corona Barathri was set up in 2016 by Russian artist Ilya Affectvs, who also runs Speculum Diaboli Records. The project released a string of works through Noctivagant and Speculum Diaboli Records before “Atra Mors,” a 2020 split album with Poland’s Paranoia Inducta, inspired by the historical plague. In late 2021, Corona Barathri released “Lapis Sacrificialis,” its first work for Cyclic Law, featuring guest vocalists including New Zealand’s Chthonia and France’s Darkrama.

“Immersio in Caliginem” continues that relationship with Cyclic Law and expands the project’s lineup for the first time, with Tania Geisler and Alexandra Fauho joining as members alongside Ilya Affectvs.

items.title: “Forever in the Blood Moon” — Berlin Darkwavers Night Nail Head Out on a Ghoulish Commute in Video for “Feelings Are Monsters”
items.summary: Thoughts of dread for the living. Pandering with the queen of sorrow. Pandering to the mirrors of no tomorrow. Depression can turn a trip to the corner shop into such… The post “Forever in the Blood Moon” — Berlin Darkwavers Night Nail Head Out on a Ghoulish C
items.fullText:
Thoughts of dread for the living.

Pandering with the queen of sorrow.

Pandering to the mirrors of no tomorrow.

Depression can turn a trip to the corner shop into such a long negotiation with yourself that the place ends up closing long before you’ve picked up your keys. On “Feelings Are Monsters,” Berlin’s Night Nail give that dread seven eyes and seven legs. Brandon Robert counts them off as though taking inventory might make the damn thing easier to deal with.

Once upon a time, Robert was scraping by as a hired bassist in Hollywood, selling other people’s demos on the street, when a bandmate who put great stock in lucky numbers told him to “cheer up.” “It was degrading,” Robert says of those days. “But, we had to eat. Super dark times.”

“I decided that day to never play for someone else’s dream again,” Robert recalls. “I started recording my own music. I learned the hard way that no one tells your story for you. My bandmates actually did support me in my breakaway dream and ended up helping me tremendously with making my first singles and videos. But, I learned it’s really all on you to make it happen and rightfully so.”

That faith in lucky numbers has a sour afterlife in the refrain, where Robert sings, “Luck won’t change your number.” The track opens in a clatter, with bright flecks of guitar sticking out of the noise. Once the drums snap into time, the guitar winds through the sort of uneasy melody The Comsat Angels used to make sound inevitable, while the bassline lays down a gothic rock groove. A little over a minute in, Ruby Mai’s saxophone takes over from Robert’s low recitation. He comes back with his voice raised, then lets it sink in again, deeper, as he draws out his ode to the “queen of sorrow.” A rubbery bass break gives way to another round of counting before the guitar takes the song out.

Director Ilija Gavrilenko and editor Jean De Oliveira keep returning to the band under blue light, with black wisps spreading across the frame. Between those shots, a skull-faced figure in a wide black hat rides a lime-green scooter and lopes around a courtyard carpeted with fallen leaves. It looks like somebody sent a horror-movie ghoul out to run an errand.

Watch the video for “Feelings Are Monsters” below.

Night Nail formed in Los Angeles in 2013 and moved to Berlin before releasing their 2018 debut, LA Demons, on Cleopatra Records. March To Autumn followed on Cold Transmission in 2020, and Metropolis released Fates Explained in 2023. William Faith and Sven Wolff handled mixing and post-production on Night Nail’s fourth studio album, Infinite Fountain. Wolff worked on “Feelings Are Monsters” at Berlin’s Cosmonaut Studio, with Night Nail co-producing and Alex Lee contributing additional synths.

Infinite Fountain was released on November 6, 2026, on Icy Cold Records, and the vinyl edition follows on December 4. Listen below and order the album here

items.title: Bruce Gilbert’s ‘London Orbital’ gets screenings and talks in December and January
items.summary: The Hotel has scheduled 'London Orbital' screenings and Chris Petit and Iain Sinclair talks in London from 1 December to 14 January.
items.fullText:
English musician Bruce Gilbert’s sound work “London Orbital” is the focus of a series of screenings and talks in London this December and January, staged by The Hotel ahead of the vinyl edition’s release on 27 November 2026.

The events pair screenings of “London Orbital,” the 2002 Channel 4 film the album soundtracks, with talks on post-cinema from the film’s directors, Chris Petit and Iain Sinclair. Further dates are set to be announced in 2027.

  • 1 December – Chris Petit and Iain Sinclair talk on post-cinema, Barking
  • 2 December – “London Orbital” screening with a Petit and Sinclair Q&A, Barking
  • 3 December – “London Orbital” screening at The Cinema Museum, London
  • 5 December – “London Orbital” screening with a Petit and Sinclair talk, Conditions
  • 14 January – “London Orbital” screening, The Horse Hospital, London

“London Orbital” takes its title from Sinclair’s 2000 book of the same name, which traced the author’s two-year walk around the M25, the motorway that circles London. Petit drove the route instead, combining early digital video with CCTV footage. The Hotel presents the result as “a sound film” rather than a conventional soundtrack, with the LP’s booklet carrying stills from the film alongside new essays by Petit and Sinclair. Side-Line covered the vinyl release’s announcement in full, including its credits and tracklist, when it was first set for 27 November.

Gilbert performed with The Hotel at Café OTO in London in October 2026, alongside Rocheman and Finn Kennedy.

About Bruce Gilbert

Bruce Clifford Gilbert was born on 18 May 1946 in Watford, England. He studied graphic design at Leicester Polytechnic until 1971, then worked as an abstract painter before taking a job in 1975 as an audio-visual technician at Watford College of Art and Design, where he began experimenting with tape loops and oscillators in the college’s recording studio.

Gilbert and fellow Watford student Colin Newman formed a short-lived group called Overload; in the summer of 1976, Graham Lewis and Robert Gotobed joined them to form Wire. Wire released three albums between 1976 and 1979 – “Pink Flag,” “Chairs Missing” and “154” – before disbanding after a show at London’s Electric Ballroom in early 1980. During Wire’s inactive years, Gilbert and Lewis worked together as Cupol, Dome, P’o and Duet Emmo. Gilbert later rejoined Wire for its reunions and left the band for good in 2004, since focusing on solo work and collaborations with visual artists and other experimental musicians, released through Mute, Touch and Editions Mego.

Gilbert’s “London Orbital,” his sound work for Chris Petit and Iain Sinclair’s 2002 film, is released on vinyl by The Hotel on 27 November 2026, with the December and January screenings and talks accompanying that release.

items.title: Kraftwerk To Make ‘Glastonbury’ Debut As Massive Attack, Underworld And Primal Scream Join 2027 Lineup
items.summary: Kraftwerk will play Glastonbury for the first time in 2027, alongside Massive Attack, Underworld, Primal Scream and CHVRCHES at Worthy Farm.
items.fullText:
Glastonbury Festival has revealed the first names for its 2027 edition, running June 23-27, 2027 at Worthy Farm, Pilton, Somerset. Alongside headliners Sam Fender, Harry Styles and Billie Eilish, with Cher in the traditional Sunday Legends slot, the announcement brings Kraftwerk to Glastonbury for the first time, joined by Massive Attack, Underworld, Primal Scream, CHVRCHES, The xx and Hot Chip. The festival returns after a scheduled fallow year in 2026.

Kraftwerk make their Glastonbury debut

Kraftwerk will headline the West Holts Stage, their first Glastonbury appearance more than five decades after the group began working with synthesizer-based composition. Founded in Düsseldorf by Ralf Hütter and Florian Schneider, Kraftwerk’s catalogue, including “Autobahn” (1974), “Trans-Europe Express” (1977), “The Man-Machine” (1978) and “Computer World” (1981), established a vocabulary of repetition, mechanical precision and human-machine interaction that synthpop, techno, electro and EBM artists drew on afterward. The band’s audiovisual performances, combining geometric imagery, synchronised visuals and its recurring robotic presentation, have remained part of its identity since. Kraftwerk’s back catalogue has been the subject of a long-running EU sampling dispute, and a pair of early broadcast recordings surfaced on unofficial releases in 2025.

Massive Attack bring Bristol’s darker electronic lineage

Massive Attack return to Worthy Farm with a catalogue that moved beyond the trip-hop tag attached to it early on. “Blue Lines” (1991) and “Protection” (1994) introduced a spacious, bass-heavy sound; “Mezzanine” (1998) pushed the group toward distorted guitars and a darker atmosphere that influenced alternative electronic music afterward. The band’s live shows combine political messaging and documentary imagery with the music itself. Massive Attack played a plant-based, eco-focused show in Manchester in 2025, and released “Boots On The Ground,” a collaboration with Tom Waits, in April 2026, their first new track in six years.

Underworld, Primal Scream, CHVRCHES and The xx

Underworld’s Karl Hyde and Rick Smith have spent three decades working across techno, progressive electronics and ambient textures; “dubnobasswithmyheadman” (1994) and “Second Toughest In The Infants” (1996) established a reputation for long, gradually-built compositions that their live shows continue to develop instead of replaying.

Primal Scream’s catalogue runs from the dance-inflected “Screamadelica” to “XTRMNTR,” an album that pairs distorted guitars and aggressive rhythms with confrontational production. CHVRCHES return with their fifth studio album, “All The King’s Men,” due January 22, 2027, their first full-length since “Screen Violence” (2021). The xx bring a sparser sound, pairing guitar, bass and electronics with understated vocals.

The bill also includes Hot Chip, Saint Etienne, FKA twigs, The Avalanches, Bonobo, Basement Jaxx, Nia Archives, Chase & Status, Robyn and Young Fathers, with further acts, stage allocations and performance details to be announced in the coming months.

Glastonbury Festival 2027 23-27 June 2027, Worthy Farm, Pilton, Somerset, UK

About Glastonbury Festival

Glastonbury Festival of Contemporary Performing Arts takes place annually (with scheduled fallow years) at Worthy Farm in Pilton, Somerset, and has run since 1970. The 2027 edition follows a fallow year in 2026 and is scheduled for June 23-27, 2027. Confirmed acts beyond the Pyramid Stage headliners include Kraftwerk, making their first festival appearance; Massive Attack, Underworld, Primal Scream, CHVRCHES, The xx, Hot Chip, Saint Etienne, FKA twigs, The Avalanches, Bonobo, Basement Jaxx, Nia Archives, Chase & Status, Robyn and Young Fathers.

items.title: Metropolis Records releases charity compilation ‘Calm Within The Storm’
items.summary: Metropolis Records released the charity compilation "Calm Within The Storm" on November 18, 2026, benefiting Detroit recovery group Passenger.
items.fullText:
Metropolis Records released the charity compilation “Calm Within The Storm” on November 18, 2026. The 20-track album draws on the rosters of Metropolis, Artoffact, COP International and Distortion Productions, with contributions from The Birthday Massacre, Then Comes Silence, PIG vs Psyclon Nine, Assemblage 23, Magic Wands, Hunter As A Horse, Electric Six, Caustic, In Letter Form and Rohn Lederman, among others. All proceeds go to Passenger, a Detroit-based addiction recovery support organization founded a decade ago by Christopher Tait of Electric Six.

Metropolis Records’ own Haulix promo page lists a “Radio Impact” date of 18 November 2026 alongside a separate, later “Release” date of 21 January 2027. Bandcamp, Spotify and the label’s own social media posts all list the album, and each of its individual tracks, as released on November 18, 2026.

The compilation is dedicated to Dave Heckman, who founded Metropolis Records in 1993 and ran the label until his death in 2022. It was compiled by his daughter, current label manager Nina Heckman. The cover artwork is by photographer Reuben Wu, formerly of Ladytron.

items.title: Profit Prison announces ‘Why Art Thou Wroth? And Why Is Thy Countenance Fallen?’ LP
items.summary: Profit Prison announces "Why Art Thou Wroth? And Why Is Thy Countenance Fallen?," a new LP on Avant! pressed in two limited vinyl editions.
items.fullText:
Profit Prison, the solo dark disco and EBM project of Seattle musician Parker Lautensleger, has announced a new album, “Why Art Thou Wroth? And Why Is Thy Countenance Fallen?,” on Avant! The LP follows Profit Prison’s debut full-length, “Gilt,” and is pressed in two limited vinyl editions of 250 copies each, one on transparent yellow vinyl and one on black vinyl.

Profit Prison’s own Bandcamp page lists the album as releasing digitally on January 20, 2027. Avant!’s distribution sheet lists the two vinyl editions as shipping on 22 January 2027.

The album’s eight tracks move between hi-NRG disco beats, synthpop and dark ambient passages, with Lautensleger’s reverberated vocals running through all of them. Avant! describes the record as combining the shorter tracks of Profit Prison’s first two EPs with the longer, more elaborate songs on “Gilt.”

A video accompanies “In Memoriam,” the album’s first single.

Tracklist

  1. A Good Harvest Year
  2. In Memoriam
  3. A Misanthrope
  4. Sobriquet
  5. Laughingstock
  6. Threnody
  7. Pietà
  8. Caroline

About Profit Prison

Seattle, Washington musician Parker Lautensleger has recorded as Profit Prison since conceiving the project in 2016, exploring themes of isolation, estrangement and paranoia through synthpop and post-punk, with industrial drum programming running underneath. Lautensleger also performs in Anteinferno, Bhereg, Victims Panel and Excarnated Entity. Profit Prison’s debut release came out through Dominick Fernow’s Hospital Productions in 2017, followed by two EPs and the full-length album “Gilt” on Avant! “Why Art Thou Wroth? And Why Is Thy Countenance Fallen?” is Profit Prison’s second full-length for the label.

items.title: J Wølf: the long road to ‘Tainted Scent’ featuring Frank M. Spinath
items.summary: J Wølf's Jan Dewulf tells Karo Kratochwil how "Tainted Scent," featuring Frank M. Spinath of Seabound, grew from a 2017 studio session into a finished EP.
items.fullText:
Jan Dewulf is probably best known for Mildreda, the Belgian electro-industrial project rooted in the harsher, psychologically charged traditions of dark electronics. His work as J Wølf, however, reveals another side of his musical personality, one driven by a fascination with electronic dance music, melody and the freedom to experiment beyond his better-known project’s aesthetic boundaries. The four-track EP “Tainted Scent,” featuring Frank M. Spinath of Seabound and Edge of Dawn, released on 13 November 2026 through Dewulf’s own Wølf Productions imprint, is an example of that creative independence. Spacious synthesizer arrangements, fluid rhythms and an expressive vocal performance give the title composition a cinematic quality, while the rest of the EP takes a more direct, club-oriented approach. Behind the music lies a story of spontaneous inspiration, forgotten recordings and a collaboration that took years to reach its final form. Karo Kratochwil spoke with Dewulf for Side-Line about how it came together.

Dewulf makes no secret of the distinction between his projects. “Musically, it’s quite different from Mildreda, of course. J Wølf is my little playground where I can freely explore my love for electronic dance / techno / EBM / … music.” That description of J Wølf as a playground seems especially apt here, not because the music lacks seriousness or compositional ambition, but because it lets Dewulf approach electronic production with an openness that would be harder to accommodate within Mildreda’s established identity. The synthesizers are warmer, the rhythms less confrontational, and the arrangements leave room for melodic development.

His own reference points shed light on the EP’s character. “For this EP: think of the warmth and organic electronics of Syntax, the infectious energy of early Underworld and those irresistible Fluke hooks. Add Frank’s melancholic voice to the mix, and the result has an emotional depth that I personally really love.” Those influences are recognisable in the flowing electronic sequences, the basslines and the ease with which the music moves between dance-oriented momentum and more introspective passages. Yet “Tainted Scent” does not sound like an attempt to reproduce an earlier period’s electronic music. Dewulf draws on its vocabulary without turning nostalgic, pairing an instinctive sense of rhythm with a production style that favours clarity and subtle shifts in atmosphere over complexity.

The title track carries the EP. Frank M. Spinath’s voice combines depth, strength and emotional openness, giving the music an almost panoramic dimension. There is a melancholic romanticism in his delivery, not sentimental and not reliant on dramatic gestures, that comes through in his measured phrasing and the tone variations that suggest longing, tenderness and a certain emotional distance without reducing the song to one feeling. His voice inhabits Dewulf’s arrangement comfortably: the synthesizers establish a broad harmonic landscape, and an understated rhythmic pulse lets the vocal melody unfold without competing for attention.

Knowing how those vocals were originally recorded makes the finished track more intriguing. As Dewulf explained to Kratochwil in correspondence, the collaboration was never planned as a formal recording project. “Quite some time ago (a few years in fact), I was playing Frank a few demos of mine. He suddenly felt inspired to sing something, and before we knew it, we were recording vocals. Completely spontaneous, without any real plan.” The recordings were then set aside, along with another composition that would eventually land on the same EP. “But as it sometimes goes, life got in the way. The recordings of ‘Tainted Scent’ ended up gathering dust on a hard drive. The same happened to ‘Here to Stay,’ another track dating back to those days (featuring my own vocals).”

Even Dewulf and Spinath no longer remember exactly when the original session took place. When Dewulf revisited the recordings recently, a photograph from his studio offered a clue. “Frank actually asked me this week when we recorded those vocals. I had to look it up myself, and I’m going by the photo I’ve attached. I honestly have no idea exactly when we recorded the vocals for ‘Tainted Scent,’ back when it wasn’t even a proper song yet.” The photo, showing Spinath behind a microphone in Dewulf’s studio, turned out to date back to 2017, captioned at the time: “It’s happening #jwolf #spinath.”

The EP’s finished form took shape later, during the pandemic lockdown, a period Dewulf remembers as one of unusual creative productivity across several of his projects at once. “2020 was also a year when my creativity absolutely exploded. I finished a Your Life On Hold album, wrote and completed albums for both Mildreda and Dive, and somehow managed to squeeze in ‘Here to Stay’ as well. I’m almost certain that, during that same mad rush of inspiration, I finally shaped ‘Tainted Scent’ into the track it is today.” Despite that gap between the original vocal session and the finished production, Spinath’s phrasing and Dewulf’s arrangement complement each other closely, with no audible sign of ideas assembled years apart.

The delay also gives the release a personal weight for Dewulf, not least because of Spinath’s relative absence from recent music. “I always thought it was a shame that nothing ever happened with those songs. So I’m really happy they’re finally seeing the light of day. Especially since Frank’s wonderful, unmistakable voice has been absent from new music for quite some time.”

The EP’s second original track, “Here to Stay,” shows another side of J Wølf, with Dewulf himself on vocals and a more direct, dance-oriented approach built on buoyant synthesizer sequences and melodic hooks that occasionally brush against synthpop. The accompanying FUCKBOT remix, produced by Mario Vaerewijck, pushes the track into harder territory, dismantling its melodic accessibility through clipped vocal manipulations, sharper textures and more mechanical sequencing. A radio edit of “Tainted Scent” closes the EP, with a shorter run time that brings the vocal melody and rhythm into tighter focus.

About J Wølf

J Wølf is the solo electronic project of Belgian musician Jan Dewulf, who also records as Mildreda. He releases through his own imprint, Wølf Productions, and previously issued the digital EP “Tekno Body Muzik Part I.” His latest EP, “Tainted Scent,” released on 13 November 2026, features Frank M. Spinath of Seabound and Edge of Dawn on the title track, Dewulf’s own vocals on “Here to Stay,” and a remix of that song by FUCKBOT, the techno project of Mario Vaerewijck, known for his work with Insekt and Suicide Commando. “Tainted Scent” is available digitally on Bandcamp.

items.title: kinGeorg interview: ‘Hjerter Som Fryser’, Stephan Groth and the road to 2027
items.summary: kinGeorg (Kim Georg Lunde) talks to Side-Line about "Hjerter Som Fryser," Stephan Groth's "Heroes" remix and his debut album, due on Apollon Records in 2027.
items.fullText:
Norwegian musician Kim Georg Lunde records as kinGeorg, writing dark rock songs about love, loss and complicated relationships. His latest single, “Hjerter Som Fryser,” explores a relationship losing its warmth, and precedes his first full-length kinGeorg album, due in 2027 on Apollon Records. Britta Pirkko spoke with Lunde for Side-Line about the single, his years fronting Sørgekåpe, singing in Norwegian, his collaboration with Stephan Groth of Apoptygma Berzerk, and what comes next.

kinGeorg on love, Apollon Records and the road to 2027

Britta: Kim, let’s start before kinGeorg. You spent years fronting Sørgekåpe, releasing albums, touring and sharing stages with bands like Seigmen and CC Cowboys. Then, in 2019, you went solo. Had you been considering that move for a while, or did you simply want to do things your own way? And looking back, is there anything you miss about being in a band?

Kim: I guess it came down to having different ambitions, both musically and artistically, and wanting to express myself in my own way.

Yes, there are definitely things I miss about being in a band. But at the same time, kinGeorg feels like a band too, since I work with regular musicians. kinGeorg is one big circus, like a family, so that pretty much fills the gap. Haha!

Britta: Love, loss and complicated relationships keep finding their way into your songs. Your latest single, “Hjerter Som Fryser,” deals with love slowly growing cold, but there’s still a bit of hope in there. How much of your own life ends up in your lyrics? Have you ever written something so personal that you hesitated to let anyone hear it?

Kim: Yes, there have been several times when I haven’t dared to tell the truth about my own life. It’s taken me many years to open up about some of the things I’ve experienced.

At the same time, I love writing in metaphors. A song or a lyric can mean one thing to one person and something completely different to someone else.

But yes, I’m definitely quite obsessed with the subject of love. Almost a little too obsessed, and sometimes that even scares me.

Britta: You’ve stuck with Norwegian, even as your music reaches listeners outside Scandinavia. Have you ever seriously considered singing in English, or would that mean losing something important? Personally, I think music can get under your skin without understanding a single word. How do you see it?

Kim: I’ve considered singing in English several times, but it just wouldn’t be kinGeorg. For me, it would take away the very soul of kinGeorg’s music.

It would be like having a girlfriend who normally speaks Norwegian, and then suddenly she starts speaking Chinese. That would be pretty strange, wouldn’t it? Haha!

Britta: You’ve worked with musicians from quite different backgrounds, including Christer Krogh, Johan Larsson, Trygve Skaug and Alex Møklebust. Do you prefer collaborators who immediately understand what you’re after, or those who challenge your ideas? Has anyone ever made you rethink a song completely?

Kim: First of all, I want to say that I’ve always been incredibly proud to work with so many talented people.

I love being challenged, and it happens all the time. I’ll even go as far as saying that kinGeorg wouldn’t be kinGeorg without many of the people I work with.

Why? Because we’re constantly building the kinGeorg universe together, based on whatever is going on inside my head.

And that’s exactly what I love about kinGeorg. Being inspired, and just as importantly, being able to inspire others.

It’s actually quite rare for a song to be completely changed, because most people in this family already understand what it’s all about.

Britta: Stephan Groth of Apoptygma Berzerk remixed your Norwegian version of Bowie and Brian Eno’s “Heroes” for Helter P.T.2. It’s quite a song to take on in the first place! What did you think when you heard Stephan’s interpretation, and did it take the track somewhere you hadn’t expected? Any chance of another collaboration, or am I getting ahead of myself?

Kim: 100 out of 100! I absolutely loved his version. And yes, it’s quite a song to take on!

I’ve always told myself that I would never do covers, but I made one exception, and most likely the only exception I’ll ever make.

At the same time, I feel that everything about this song fits perfectly into the kinGeorg universe.

Most people know how brilliant Stephan is, so I wasn’t surprised at all by how it turned out. We’re all extremely happy with the result.

As for another collaboration, no comment. 😉

We’re pretty good at surprising people. Haha!

Britta: You’ve been making music for years, so surely something has gone spectacularly wrong at some point. Or spectacularly right! What’s one moment on stage or behind the scenes that still makes you laugh, cringe or shake your head?

Kim: That would have to be the time I was on national television in Norway, on TV 2’s Good Morning Norway, together with Trygve Skaug.

I suddenly asked the entire studio out loud if we were still live on air. Well, let’s just say… we were! So the whole of Norway got to hear me wondering about that. I’ve thought about that moment a few times since!

Britta: You’ve got a new album planned for 2027, and “Hjerter Som Fryser” has already given us another taste of what’s coming. How far along are you? Is there anything you’re doing differently this time, or something you’ve wanted to try for ages but haven’t had the chance to?

Kim: The new album takes me back to my rock roots. It’s less pop-oriented, and it’s almost finished.

The team of producers and musicians involved is pretty killer! This will actually be the very first kinGeorg album, and I decided early on that I wanted it to be raw and a little dark. And yes, I’ve been digging into my love life again.

Britta: Musicians these days are expected to write, record, promote themselves, feed social media and somehow have a life as well. When are they actually supposed to make music? How do you deal with those demands? Have you ever felt like telling the whole machinery to piss off for a while? And has your idea of success changed over the years?

Kim: If there’s one thing I really don’t enjoy, it’s putting myself out there on social media like some kind of influencer. I can do a lot of crazy things, but that just isn’t really me.

At the same time, I understand that times are changing, for better or worse.

Success is also a pretty broad word. I think the whole machinery misses out on a lot, while at the same time discovering a lot of great things. I’m no god who can tell everyone what’s right or wrong here.

Personally, I just try to throw a picture out there, smile nicely, and focus on creating and releasing music that people actually want to listen to and can relate to.

Britta: So, what does 2027 have in store for kinGeorg? Anything you’re particularly excited about, or something you’ve been plotting behind the scenes that we should know about?

Kim: There’s a lot going on behind the scenes! We’ll be playing quite a few new festivals, heading over to Sweden, and we’re also working on plans for other countries.

At the same time, we’ve got the new album coming out on our new record label, Apollon Records. So yeah, I don’t think we’ll be unemployed anytime soon. Haha!

Britta: Open Mic! My favourite way to end an interview. No fixed topic, no restrictions and no journalist throwing another question at you. Anything we haven’t covered, something you’d like to get off your chest, a message to your listeners or a question you’ve always wanted someone to ask? The floor is yours.

Kim: I’m looking forward to what comes next in this world we’re living in. And maybe it’s time we stopped digging up the darkest sides of love. But then again, love has sides that most people would rather not see, or even dare to feel.

About kinGeorg

kinGeorg is the project of Norwegian musician Kim Georg Lunde, who writes dark rock songs about emotional intensity and the beautiful and destructive sides of love. Before going solo in 2019, Lunde fronted Sørgekåpe, releasing albums and touring alongside bands including Seigmen and CC Cowboys.

As kinGeorg, Lunde works with a recurring group of musicians and producers, among them Christer Krogh, Johan Larsson, Trygve Skaug and Alex Møklebust. His EP “Helter P.T.2,” which included a Norwegian-language cover of David Bowie and Brian Eno’s “Heroes” remixed by Apoptygma Berzerk’s Stephan Groth and Beranek, came out in January 2025. The single “Kjærlighets Grunge” followed in July 2026 on Apollon Records, and “Hjerter Som Fryser,” released on October 23, 2026 and recorded at Velvet Recordings with Christer Krogh producing, is the second single from kinGeorg’s upcoming debut album.

That album, kinGeorg’s first full-length, is due in 2027 on Apollon Records. Lunde describes it as a return to his rock roots, rawer and darker than his previous releases, with festival dates in Norway and Sweden planned around its release.

items.title: Years Of Denial announce ‘Suicide Disco Vol. 3’, share video for ‘Zero Fucks Given’
items.summary: Years Of Denial will release "Suicide Disco Vol. 3" on December 4, 2026 via Veyl, and have shared a video for "Zero Fucks Given".
items.fullText:
French-Czech darkwave duo Years Of Denial will release their new album, “Suicide Disco Vol. 3”, on December 4, 2026 via Veyl. The twelve-track record follows the group’s “Love Cuts” EP, and arrives with a video for the track “Zero Fucks Given”.

“Suicide Disco Vol. 3” continues the series Years Of Denial opened with their 2019 debut album “Suicide Disco” and followed with “Suicide Disco Vol. 2” in 2023. The new album is being issued as a digital download and as a gatefold 2LP that includes an A2 poster of the cover artwork; no CD edition has been announced. All twelve tracks were written, produced and mixed by Jérôme Tcherneyan and Barkosina Hanusova at Ark of Noise, with guitar on four of the songs, including “Zero Fucks Given”, played by Antoni Nightingale Ripper and recorded at Studio L’OndeNue in Menglon. The album was mastered by Thomas Feriero at Hidden Mountain in Milan and cut by Andreas Kauffelt at Schnittstelle in Berlin, with cover photography by Latex Lucifer and inside photography by Aylo.

The tracklist runs: “Naked”, “So Emotional”, “Too Bad”, “Hysterical”, “We Operate On Each Other”, “Listen Up”, “Zero Fucks Given”, “Fear of Life”, “Beauty Is a Curse”, “With Love From Ostrava”, “Heroine” and “Dying Breed”. “We Operate On Each Other” previously appeared as a standalone single on Death & Leisure before this album placed it in the running order.

“Suicide Disco Vol. 3” is available to pre-order on Bandcamp as a digital album and as a 2LP.

About Years Of Denial

Years Of Denial is a duo founded in 2016 by French musician Jérôme Tcherneyan and Czech singer and lyricist Barkosina Hanusova. Tcherneyan previously drummed for the British act Piano Magic and has produced music since the late 1990s; Hanusova is also a performance artist and poet. The pair builds on hardware and dub devices, pairing cold wave and EBM with Hanusova’s detached vocal delivery.

Years Of Denial’s debut album “Suicide Disco” appeared in 2019 on Death & Leisure and Pinkman, followed by “Suicide Disco Vol. 2” in 2023. The duo signed to Veyl for the “Love Cuts” EP, reviewed on Side-Line in 2025, and stay with the label for “Suicide Disco Vol. 3”, due December 4, 2026, with “Zero Fucks Given” as its first video.

items.title: Seattle Dungeon Synthpop Project PROFIT PRISON Asks What the Living Owe the Dead in Video for “In Memoriam”
items.summary: Their lives felt somewhat sound Though they’d lost control of the outskirts of their town and I loathe to tell you how it ends so in silence we bow our… The post Seattle Dungeon Synthpop Project PROFIT PRISON Asks What the Living Owe the Dead in Video for “In
items.fullText:
Their lives felt somewhat sound
Though they’d lost control of the outskirts of their town
and I loathe to tell you how it ends
so in silence we bow our heads

There’s something profoundly rotten about a world where people can disappear, families can be destroyed, and the surviving witnesses are expected to carry on buying groceries and paying their miserable bills while history quietly buries the evidence. Human civilization has developed an extraordinary talent for committing atrocities, commemorating the dead, and finding fresh excuses to repeat the process. Somewhere in this grand procession of moral bankruptcy, Seattle’s Profit Prison has found sufficient inspiration to write a disco song about the unbearable weight of collective guilt.

The solo project of Parker Lautensleger, whose musical history includes Anteinferno, Bhereg, Victims Panel, and Excarnated Entity, has spent nearly a decade exploring the more psychologically disturbed possibilities of electronic pop. His latest single, In Memoriam, taken from the forthcoming album Why art thou wroth? And why is thy countenance fallen?, sounds like Bronski Beat wandering into a particularly unpleasant historical reckoning, with electronic pioneer Gershon Kingsley conducting the proceedings from behind an enormous bank of synthesizers.

The arrangement possesses a strange, almost indecent sweetness. Synthesizers trace delicate melodic figures above a measured electronic rhythm, their crystalline repetitions creating the impression of a forgotten European dance record rescued from somebody’s flooded basement. Lautensleger sings with a trembling, distant resignation, his voice occupying the uncomfortable space between Neil Young’s wounded sincerity and the exquisite emotional distress of early synthpop by Das Kabinette, Depeche Mode, and others you might find on the Some Bizzare Compilation. Every syllable seems burdened by information its owner would dearly prefer to forget.

And what dreadful information it is. The lyrics describe a family whose apparently stable existence has been overturned by events unfolding near a border, where some unspecified act of violence has left questions that nobody seems willing to answer. Children inherit uncertainty, the dead receive their solemn acknowledgments, and the living are forced to contemplate the possibility that their own moral identities have been built upon carefully maintained ignorance. The song’s repeated interrogations grow increasingly desperate, suggesting a confrontation with somebody whose participation in an atrocity has become impossible to dismiss. Beneath the delicate electronic flourishes lies the hideous proposition that ordinary people can commit extraordinary acts of cruelty and subsequently spend entire lifetimes inventing explanations for themselves.

In Memoriam‘s synthesizers maintain their patient, hypnotic progression while the words wander into the ugliest corners of human responsibility. You could conceivably dance to this record, which raises some rather uncomfortable questions about the emotional usefulness of disco. Lautensleger leaves those questions unanswered, however, allowing the music to continue its beautiful, merciless rotations while the accumulated weight of memory threatens to crush everything beneath it.

The video takes on a philosophical matter, as though we’re prisoners in Plato’s cave, watching distorted projections of events whose true nature remains somewhere beyond our comprehension. The road stretches onward, the lights assault our vision, and every image seems to conceal a fragment of some dreadful revelation.

items.fullText:
At the edge of the abyss I stand
Into the depths I am drawn
The future without me
Troglobite in bizarre light.

A red light in a fog-filled nightclub lets you see who’s beside you on the dance floor. In a limestone cave, a lamp can reveal an olm, a pale salamander that lives underground. For Hanover-based “singer-doomwriter” David Barteczko, who first played as KOSMOBERKH on an open stage in Oldenburg, there’s a kinship between those two kinds of light. He puts them side by side on Troglobiten in Absonderlicht, a title he translates as “Troglobites in Secluded Light.”

Released November 6, 2026, on Barteczko’s own Zeichenlos Records, the ten-track album is his first since 2018’s oneiroi, which came out under the name Mosaikh. A club gives young people somewhere to make things together and try out how they want to live. Barteczko’s characters are looking for that kind of room under political and economic pressure. Pandemic isolation, war, a changing climate and the lure of conspiracy theories and parallel lives online form the backdrop to the album’s loosely connected episodes.

That first stage was Craftwork Café at Oldenburg’s Metro discotheque, where Barteczko tried out songs between 2011 and 2013. He describes those sets in terms of Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring and Joy Division’s “Dead Souls,” both evoked by a single acoustic guitar. The 2014 demo Urbild began his recording partnership with Alex Pojda. Barteczko set his voice aside for the instrumental post-rock of Dim Nachttag in 2016 and took up singing again with Mosaikh, the electric trio whose songs about belonging drew on his experience as a Polish migrant.

During the break from KOSMOBERKH, Barteczko played in prog-doom band CMDR RIKR and post-rock group BRUECKEN. He returned to the stage in May 2024, opening for Extra Life at Cadillac in Oldenburg with cellist Jann Michael Engel, whose credits include Anne Clark and Mila Mar. The pair recorded the cello in Göttingen, and Barteczko tracked his vocals, synths, percussion and effects at home. Most of the guitars were recorded at Holodeck Studio, where Pojda co-produced the album with Barteczko and mixed and mastered it.

Barteczko’s acoustic guitar and Engel’s cello are at the center of the record. Synths, electronic percussion and field recordings carry the arrangements into ethereal wave and chamber doom. Barteczko’s reference points range from early Dead Can Dance and Scott Walker’s Scott 4 to David Bowie’s The Man Who Sold the World and Peter Hammill’s In Camera.

Deep strums and a low cello line set the instrumental “Fiz Oblon” in motion. The opener, issued October 16 as the fourth and final advance single, has the pace of a walk by lantern light, with the drums moving steadily beneath the acoustic riffs and Alex Pojda’s bass carrying the rounded weight of gothic rock. Engel takes the cello higher against the guitar before a rubbery industrial darkwave beat takes over for a spell. The cello returns to pick up the melody. The piece is named for the Bippen discotheque where Barteczko developed his taste in music, and he dedicates it to the memory of Pai and Hage. In the single notes, he credits clubs like this one with bringing him to music and to people who stayed in his life.

Barteczko first sings on “Asche meiner Jugend,” in a high, unhurried voice over gentle acoustic guitar. The lyric puts crimson clouds in a skylight and stroboscopes in a room he once knew. He can picture it well enough to feel like a stranger there now. Reverb carries off the ends of his phrases in the chorus, and Engel comes in with a low, grieving cello line. The two instruments find a brisk folk rhythm as Barteczko sings with more force. The quicker rhythm gives him a few bars to dance on the ashes of his youth and ask if anyone can see him glow.

A light chime moves through “Sterngeworden” like bells attached to someone’s dancing feet. The acoustic guitar makes room for clear electric notes to ring, and Engel draws out one of his loveliest melodies. Barteczko’s languid delivery suggests The Replacements and The Cure. The acoustic playing has the intimacy of Nick Drake, and the electric guitar has the soft focus of dream pop. The singer looks to the past for some sense of what lies ahead. In the last lines, he hopes someone else’s longing might carry him home.

Getting home grows complicated on “Zugvogel.” Strings ripple behind the gentle acoustic strum while the cello keeps chugging along, and an electric-sounding quiver unsettles the edges of the arrangement. There’s something of The Cure’s “Catch” in the voice and the acoustic swing, set in a scene that could belong to a David Lynch film. One migrating bird loses its sense of day, night and direction. A second bird’s plumage is a business suit, and its days are a funeral procession. Those small, birdlike sounds leave the flight feeling as though it could take you from one dream, or one life, straight into the next.

There’s a dry click at the end of the guitar strokes in “Hybris.” Barteczko comes in slowly above a deep cello tone, with the deliberate phrasing of someone waking up and deciding he wants out. A brighter melody suddenly picks up the pace, then the playing shifts again into a loose, almost jazzy groove. Earlier figures reappear as quickly as the moods that brought them on. The words make a similar series of turns. One person wants to break free of himself, asks someone else to break free with him, and shudders when the thing they’ve made together breaks free in turn.

The acoustic strum on “Telegramme” sways as though it could stop between strokes, and there’s an ease to Barteczko’s delivery even as he sings about messages falling like ash and people being made to whisper obediently. Christoffer Grunau plays drums, and Udo Kirfel contributes bass. Engel holds a low, steady line before reaching up to accent individual phrases. His playing grows more melodic and climbs higher as the song closes. By then Barteczko is moving between a whisper and a shout, asking the other person to hold his hand and bracing himself for their answer.

The first single, “Stummfilm” (August 14), begins with a cello melody that nearly waltzes, the acoustic guitar keeping step. The introductory figure gives way to a gentler strum, and then the cello bears down again beneath Barteczko’s voice. In the lyric, two lives are bound up in a shared manuscript. He dips the other person’s page in ink, the paper tears, and he plays the images back in his head in silence. Guitar and cello build around him until his voice recedes. Engel takes the melody back with a little more lift to it, and the guitar falls in beside him.

The video reworks F. W. Murnau’s 1926 silent film Faust, bringing the outsized gestures of German Expressionism to the guilt and private fantasies of a relationship that has run out of words.

The second single, “Zypressen” (September 4), starts with a soft strum, a passing synth tone, and an especially tender vocal. Engel takes his time entering. Once he does, the cello zigzags across the guitar part and elaborates on its own melody while the singing pauses. The bow moves faster, and the synth tones darken. When the cello drops away, the voice and guitar briefly have the space to themselves. Engel comes back to carry the melody under the singing, and rain enters over gentle strumming. The close brings distorted electric guitar alongside the cello, and Barteczko’s voice sounds much farther away.

The song follows an exhausted nurse through an understaffed hospital ward, where she tends to cypresses in place of patients. The applause that keeps her awake at home recalls the people who took to their windows to clap for hospital staff during the pandemic. For the video, original art sits alongside paintings, notably the work of Swiss Symbolist Arnold Böcklin, whose cypresses take on an uneasy motion.

The instrumental “Oras Bad” opens with a rush of sound and a chime-like jangle. A soft, guitar-like figure trails into reverb above a low electronic hum. As the rush grows louder, that low tone holds its place with the clarity of one detail in a dream. Ora’s name returns when Barteczko calls for rain on the closing track.

Christof Schlaak’s high piano notes fall far apart in “Petrichor,” the album closer and third single, released September 25. They land like the first drops of rain on stone, with a soft acoustic strum underneath. Engel’s cello falls into step with Barteczko’s aching vocal for a few bars, then moves off on its own. When the electric guitar swells, the space between those sparse notes fills up with cello and piano over Grunau’s drums and Kirfel’s bass. The arrangement feels poised for a downpour. It ends with the electric guitar easing off into something close to a sigh.

Barteczko had planned to end the record with an instrumental until, as he recalls, “the first line escaped my lips.” The person singing it stands at the edge of an abyss, imagining a future that will go on without him. Then he catches the scent of rain. After an album full of people straining to get a word through, “Do you smell the rain?” is a question anyone standing beside him could answer.

The black gatefold vinyl is limited to 120 copies, and both the LP and the digital download are exclusive to Bandcamp. The album is also available on streaming services, including Spotify.

items.title: Venin Carmin announces ‘Of Saints And Vermin’ album, due 29 January 2027
items.summary: Venin Carmin's new album 'Of Saints And Vermin' is due 29 January 2027 via Icy Cold Records, the French dark pop act's first LP since the 'Toxic Legends' EP.
items.fullText:
French project Venin Carmin will release Of Saints And Vermin on 29 January 2027 through Icy Cold Records. The 12-track album is Venin Carmin’s first full-length since the “Toxic Legends” EP, released a little over three years ago. Venin Carmin is the solo project of Lula Borgia, who is based in South-East France and handles vocals, bass, synthesisers and lyrics.

“Of Saints And Vermin” was recorded and mixed by Nicolas César and mastered by Bruno Gruel at Elektra Mastering. Arrangements are credited to Borgia and Sammy Guell, with artwork and promotional photography by Faallaway.

Borgia describes her own sound as “trve dark pop,” a self-coined genre she says draws on industrial, trap and trip-hop elements while moving past the post-punk, goth and coldwave scenes Venin Carmin came up in. She sums up the album’s style in her own words: “hybrid, poisonous, and sovereign.” On “Of Saints And Vermin,” that range runs from the industrial opener “Hatefully Yours” through the trap-inflected “She Calls It War” to the trip-hop-leaning “Little Joy & Karma” and “Salt & Paper.”

Borgia stated: “For this album, I spent much less time worrying about sticking to a specific style. Instead, I figured that, come what may, I would manage to infuse this pop music with a certain darkness. Or, if not darkness, perhaps a sense of irreverence. Sometimes, I feel as though I’m perceiving this music through tinted glasses; I’m not sure if they’re black, red, or pink, but I definitely need to make the music my own, to imbue it with a kind of irony and cynicism. I wouldn’t call it ‘bubblegum pop.’ If it had a flavor, it would probably be licorice.”

The album’s title plays on the name Borgia uses for Venin Carmin’s fanbase. She stated: “I find it interesting that the opposition isn’t limited to the semantics of ‘saints’ versus ‘profane’, or the dominant versus the dominated. It can also be heard in the very sounds of the words. The term ‘Saints’ is meant to represent virtuous, immaculate individuals; yet, one might notice that the word itself sounds ‘perfidious’. It carries a sibilant, hissing quality. Conversely, ‘Vermin’, a word typically burdened with negative connotations, strikes my ears as far more rounded, perhaps even ‘cute’. Thus, in Of Saints And Vermin, there is a discordance between the meaning of the words and the way they are pronounced.” Borgia has long called her own fanbase “Vermin.”

The album’s tracklist is: “The Vow: Vengeance” (Intro), “Hatefully Yours,” “I Meant Every Word” (Interlude), “She Calls It War,” “Little Joy & Karma,” “Salt & Paper,” “Psychotic,” “The Egoistic Savior of Lost Causes” (Interlude), “Lady Plague,” “Keine Möglichkeit,” “Vermin” and “She Waited And No One Came” (Outro).

About Venin Carmin

Venin Carmin is the solo project of Lula Borgia, based in South-East France. The project’s debut album, “Glam Is Gone,” was released in 2015 as a new-wave and psychedelic-wave-rock record; Side-Line reviewed the release at the time. Venin Carmin has since moved toward a darker, electronic-leaning sound, releasing the “Toxic Legends” EP a little over three years before “Of Saints And Vermin.”

With “Of Saints And Vermin,” due 29 January 2027 on Icy Cold Records, Borgia continues under the self-styled “trve dark pop” banner, combining industrial, trap and trip-hop elements across 12 tracks that she describes as built around themes of betrayal, vengeance and reclaimed power.

Dancing Plague is the work of Conor Knowles, who has released seven full-length albums and several EPs as the project since launching it in 2015. Dancing Plague is the dark electro solo project of Portland, Oregon-based musician Conor Knowles, active since 2015. The project has released seven full-length albums and several EPs, including “Domain” and “Elogium,” building a catalog that pairs EBM-style rhythms with synth-pop hooks.

The project’s prior single, “Demonizer,” released with aux animaux in August 2025, and 2024 album, “Elogium,” preceded “Endlessness,” out via Artoffact Records on 5 February 2027 as the project’s latest full-length.

items.title: Houses of Heaven – Liaison
items.summary: With ‘Liaison’, the US band Houses of Heaven delivers an electronic 90s industrial sound that captivates with its distinctive vocals.
items.fullText:
Driving old-school industrial with distinctive vocals

With ‘Liaison’, the US band Houses of Heaven deliv­er a track that imme­di­ately evokes a famil­i­ar sound. The sound is dis­tinctly old-school indus­tri­al-heavy and instantly reminds me of many 90s songs by Nine Inch Nails, from pre­cisely that peri­od when the genre was still much more elec­tron­ic in char­ac­ter. But the band isn’t merely copy­ing. The vocals sound com­pletely dif­fer­ent to Trent Reznor’s. That’s exactly what I like so much about it, because it allows Houses of Heaven to define their very own style and sound.

Lyrically, the track strikes a bal­ance, which I find fit­ting, between a life ima­gined and one actu­ally lived, whilst a sense of long­ing increas­ingly per­meates the sound. The track is part of the com­pil­a­tion ‘Inhale Vol. II’ by Breathing Records.

items.title: Claquedent Releases Single ‘Vexare’ Ahead Of Debut Album
items.summary: Paris project Claquedent released the single "Vexare", the final preview of debut album "Power Reserve", out 27 November via Phage Tapes and Solium Records.
items.fullText:
Paris-based project Claquedent released the single “Vexare”, the final preview before debut album “Power Reserve”, due on 27 November 2026 via Phage Tapes and Solium Records.

Claquedent is the project of Paul Void, a Parisian musician who has played drums for post-industrial band Stamp and currently drums for noise rock outfit Crève-Coeur, alongside work with Al-Qasar and Contrevent. “Vexare” is his first recorded lead vocal performance in a career spanning over 15 years, delivered in a deathly, black/crust style. The track also features guitar from Fabien Claes, of Lugosi and Crève-Coeur.

“Vexare” is built around a sample of Klaus Kinski’s dialogue from Werner Herzog’s 1972 film “Aguirre, the Wrath of God”. Void explained the choice: “Herzog, Jodorowsky, Alan Parker, and Terry Gilliam are the filmmakers I always return to when I’m looking for material to sample. Choosing the title ‘Vexare’, which in Latin means ‘to torment’ or ‘to disturb’, seemed a fitting echo of this Herzog film.” The title track draws on industrial, noise, dub and power electronics, with guest contributions on the album from C. of Pyrecult, MC Hank Rubeé and Faggia.

About Claquedent

Claquedent is a solo project led by Paris-based musician Paul Void, known from post-industrial band Stamp and noise rock outfit Crève-Coeur. Side-Line previously covered the announcement of debut album ‘Power Reserve’ in September 2026. The album, out 27 November 2026 via Phage Tapes and Solium Records, follows Claquedent’s 2024 mini-album “Untitled”. “Vexare” is the final single released ahead of the album’s release.

items.title: Eden Script Releases Single ‘Humans Remain’
items.summary: Belgian dark electro act Eden Script released the self-released single "Humans Remain" on 20 November 2026, the follow-up to "Still Human".
items.fullText:
Belgian dark electro act Eden Script released the single “Humans Remain” on 20 November 2026, self-released on Bandcamp, Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. The digital single runs 4:19.

“Humans Remain” combines harsh vocals, synths and a hard-hitting beat, mixing dark electro with aggrotech, EBM and industrial elements. The track is the second part of a story cycle that began with “Still Human” (2024): where that song introduced a “new” human choosing free will, “Humans Remain” follows that human to, in the act’s own words, “a choice without compromise.” Further singles continuing the story are planned for 2027.

Eden Script is the solo project of Dominique De Caluwé, who writes, records and mixes every track alone, from the first synth line to the final mix, adding vocals where a track calls for them. The project cites Suicide Commando, Hocico, VNV Nation and :wumpscut: among its influences.

About Eden Script

Eden Script is a dark electro act from Kalmthout, Belgium, active as the solo project of Dominique De Caluwé since 2023. The act has charted three times in the Deutsche Alternative Charts: “Witches dance for a dying world” reached number 8, “Still Human” reached number 14, and “Kindgott Cataclysm” reached number 15. “Humans Remain” is Eden Script’s latest single, continuing the narrative begun on “Still Human”.

items.title: Years Of Shame Share Extended Live Video For ‘Lights’
items.summary: French sadwave duo Years Of Shame released a live music video for "Lights", from their debut album "Primary", filmed at Le Point Éphémère in Paris.
items.fullText:
French sadwave duo Years Of Shame released a live music video for “Lights”, a track from their debut album “Primary”, released on 6 February 2026 via Icy Cold Records. The vinyl and CD editions of “Primary” remain available.

Years Of Shame is the duo of vocalist Berne Evol and guitarist/producer Brice Delourmel, who also performs as Giirls. Both musicians also play in the Rennes-based coldgaze band Dead. “Lights” is one of the more direct tracks on “Primary”, built on rapid-fire, hypnotic loops. Delourmel, the track’s primary composer, describes it as “bestial”.

The video shows an extended live version of the song, featuring an additional minute of music compared to the studio recording. The extended arrangement was first performed at Le Point Éphémère in Paris during a Halloween show. Visuals were directed by Aurélien Le Beau, with special effects by Mickaël Auffret, the same pairing behind the lyric video for “Heat”, the band’s first single. The footage runs through a cathode-ray tube television manipulated in real time with analog equipment, producing the clip’s glitch aesthetic.

Lyrically, “Lights” plays out as an internal dialogue. Vocalist Berne Evol has described it as a conflict between repression and release, with the song’s refrain turning that tension toward resolution rather than darkness.

French outlet Eklektik Rock reviewed “Primary”, writing: “Nostalgia and catharsis are therefore on the menu […] of this very promising first opus. So let the tears of sadwave overwhelm you!”

About Years Of Shame

Years Of Shame is a French sadwave project formed by Berne Evol and guitarist/producer Brice Delourmel, who also records as Giirls; both are also members of the Rennes-based coldgaze band Dead. The duo released their debut album, “Primary”, on 6 February 2026 via Icy Cold Records, on vinyl, CD and digital formats. The album followed the band’s first single, “Heat”, and was followed by further singles including “Trust” and “Violence”. Years Of Shame has performed across France since the album’s release, including a show at Le Point Éphémère in Paris. “Lights” is the latest track from “Primary” to receive a dedicated video.

Alex Erbacher and Per-Anders Kurenbach both bring a wealth of experience from other projects and have been active together as District 13 for several years now. The title of this new three-track EP might suggest that the songs are older material, but I found no evidence to support that assumption.

Considerable attention has also been paid to sound design, with some elements carrying a distinct vintage quality.

After listening, my only regret is that there aren’t more tracks to enjoy. This is a strong EP that I can highly recommend. (Rating:8).

items.title: Ontario’s Fear Maintenance Pushes Joy Division’s “New Dawn Fades” to its Breaking Point
items.summary: Different colours, different shades Over each, mistakes were made I took the blame A change of scene can feel like a fresh start until you catch yourself having the same… The post Ontario’s Fear Maintenance Pushes Joy Division’s “New Dawn Fades” to its Breakin
items.fullText:
Different colours, different shades
Over each, mistakes were made
I took the blame

A change of scene can feel like a fresh start until you catch yourself having the same argument in a different room. Ian Curtis opens Joy Division’s “New Dawn Fades” with a tidy list of changes, delivered with the composure of somebody who might actually manage to make them. Then somebody raises their voice, somebody cries, and a man who says he’s walked on water and run through fire can barely feel a thing. The person he’s been waiting for turns out to be himself, and by then the promise of a new dawn has shrunk to “hoping for something else.”

On Unknown Pleasures, those are the last words you hear before you have to turn the record over. “New Dawn Fades” is track five, closing the side marked “Outside.” Factory Records released Joy Division’s debut in June 1979, following sessions with Martin Hannett at Strawberry Studios in Stockport. Peter Hook’s bass line sinks as Bernard Sumner’s guitar climbs, and Curtis’s voice grows increasingly unsteady between them. When he falls silent, the guitars play on for another minute, giving you time to sit with what he’s said before “She’s Lost Control” starts on side two.

In 1995, an instrumental edit of Moby’s cover brought that unease into Michael Mann’s Heat, where it plays over Al Pacino’s freeway pursuit. The song can keep you on edge with the words gone altogether. For Burlington, Ontario, musician Colin Adams, that possibility lay in the last minute of the original. He wanted to hear what would happen if the music went on gathering force after Curtis’s last line.

Adams explains, “You can feel the emotion building in the original recording with Ian Curtis pouring his soul out, but after the vocals end the intensity of the music gradually fades giving it a feeling of resignation. So, for this cover, I wanted to explore an alternate path and use that emotional intensity as a launchpad for a sonic explosion. In particular, with all the self-loathing lyrical content, I wanted to sonically explore the sound of someone in the midst of an emotional breakdown, with all the internal confusion, struggle and pain that could come with such an experience.”

Over four months in his Burlington home studio, Adams arranged and performed the cover and handled the production, recording, mixing, and mastering himself. He makes the coda the point where the music sounds closest to coming apart.

“New Dawn Fades” came out on November 18 as the third single from Fear Maintenance. Listen to the song on Spotify here.

For the video, Adams gave that breakdown a room of its own. He conceived, shot, and edited the clip himself at home, spending another four months working with a green screen and basic lighting in a ten-by-eight-foot space in his basement. He usually shot between ten at night and two in the morning.

Adams says, “The approach for the video was to reflect the internal strife and self-loathing of the protagonist as he metaphorically beat himself up.” Watch on YouTube.

For Adams, covering Joy Division began as a way to say goodbye to a former bandmate. He was fifteen when he joined the Toronto band Face of Another as its guitarist in 1986. Their bassist, Tim Smith, introduced him to Joy Division. The two fell out and never spoke again. After Smith’s sudden death decades later, the former bandmates revisited their old songs to give his family a record of that part of his life. On the second anniversary of Smith’s death, Adams recorded “Ceremony,” going back to the band Smith had put on for him all those years earlier.

The recordings that followed “Ceremony” gave Adams a way to “simultaneously pay homage to and reimagine some of the darker iconic songs from the post-punk bands of the late 1970s and 1980s” that inspired him to become a musician. He called the project Fear Maintenance after the label that released I Live, the 1995 EP by his second Toronto band, In Faith. The group played Toronto clubs from 1990 to 1995, often at Lee’s Palace.

Adams began putting the covers out as singles with Depeche Mode’s “Stripped” in December 2025 and then went to the other side of Unknown Pleasures for “Shadowplay.” For the next single, he returned to “New Dawn Fades,” which he’d recorded and filmed before he planned to put the covers on streaming services. The video had kept finding viewers in the meantime.

items.title: “Share Your Grief” — Oakland’s Still Ruins Hold Out a Hand in Video for “Armor of Mourning”
items.summary: Take my hand And lead me home Grief can make you very good at getting people to leave you alone. Say you’re getting by in a steady enough voice and… The post “Share Your Grief” — Oakland’s Still Ruins Hold Out a Hand in Video for “Armor of Mourning” appeared f
items.fullText:
Take my hand
And lead me home

Grief can make you very good at getting people to leave you alone. Say you’re getting by in a steady enough voice and even the people who know you best start to take you at your word. Then comes an evening when all you want to hear is somebody coming up the stairs.

Put that feeling on a record in 1988, and you might get New Edition’s “Can You Stand the Rain,” with Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis leaving enough space around the beat for each voice to have its say. Sade’s “Love Is Stronger Than Pride” could lower the lights in a room just by coming on. At the last slow dance, a song like that bought you four minutes with your cheek against the padded shoulder of somebody’s jacket, trying to keep your white high-tops clear of their feet. Later, you might sit in the driveway with the engine off and the key turned just far enough to keep the late-night quiet-storm show on the radio.

At home, you could keep a blank VHS tape ready for the next time Donnie Simpson played your favorite video on BET’s Video Soul. The movies gave a record the hardest part of a conversation. Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark’s “If You Leave” scored the prom scene in Pretty in Pink. In 1989’s Say Anything…, John Cusack wore a trench coat over a Clash T-shirt and held a boombox over his head so Peter Gabriel’s “In Your Eyes” could reach a bedroom window.

Oakland, California quartet Still Ruins gives that difficult conversation the same room to breathe on “Armor Of Mourning,” the closing track of their debut LP, Through The Glass. Reverb stretches the opening drum hits, the synth bass ripples underneath, and a bright guitar part jangles into focus. The late-’80s R&B swing gives their mix of sophisti-pop, dream pop, and post-punk a slow dancer’s timing. Frankie Soto’s silky baritone holds the verse close before leaning into a melody big enough to follow somebody out of the theater.

At first he wants the door opened so people can see him on his way down. The blade in the refrain has gone weak and still cuts deep. Later, in the dark, he asks somebody to “share your grief,” offering the company he can barely admit he needs.

“As soon as we finished writing this song we knew it was going to be the final track on the record. We already wanted it to have a late 80’s RnB feel, something almost like Jam and Lewis could have written. Armor of Mourning starts off fairly emotional but by the end of the track it has the feeling of a final bow and the curtain closing: “Take my hand and lead me home.”

Eli Wengrin shot and edited the video, which looks exactly like it was captured during the period the band is trying to recreate with their sound. It encircles the band’s name with barbed wire before revealing the quartet on a wooden stage draped in black. The performance moves between warm hues and stark black-and-white close-ups, punctuated by glimpses of an overpass at dusk and an open book displaying plate armor. Beside the microphone, Soto extends an open palm, as though someone just beyond the frame might reach out and take his hand.

Watch the video for Armor of Mourning below:

Soto and multi-instrumentalist Jose Medina began writing together at a piano in Medina’s room. After years in the Central Valley DIY scene, they looked to Tears for Fears, R&B, and ’80s Spanish new wave for a different way to arrange their songs. Bassist Cyrus VandenBerghe helped turn the home-recording project into a live band, and keyboardist Marcos Gonzalez completed the quartet in 2025. They released their self-titled EP on Oakland’s Smoking Room and have shared bills with Provoker, House of Harm, and Johnny Dynamite.

Soto wrote lyrics by playing the instrumental demos and imagining what might have been happening onscreen. The quartet recorded Through The Glass at Medina’s home studio, building the arrangements with his collection of rackmount synths and digital effects. Claire Wardlaw plays saxophone over sequenced synths and 808 toms on the instrumental opener “Permanence.” Kurt Feldman of Ice Choir and The Pains of Being Pure at Heart mixed the album and contributed additional sequencing and backing vocals.

Through The Glass is out February 26, 2027, on Born Losers Records. Pre-order the album on Bandcamp or get the sea-blue vinyl from Born Losers Records.
